prize_parts.citation: for the invention of the optical lattice clock, in which atoms are trapped at a magic wavelength so that the light shift cancels, and for its development to the 10^-18 level of accuracy and stability

statement.case_for: I keep my round-1 configuration unchanged: a single prize for the optical lattice clock to Katori and Ye. After reading the whole exchange, the case still rests on what I apply to every candidate: an original invention, experimentally verified, that lets people see something they could not see before. Katori's magic-wavelength condition is that invention, because it removes the light-shift problem and makes it possible to interrogate many atoms at once without Doppler or recoil broadening. Ye's group then showed what the idea can do, with 10^-18 systematic uncertainty, clock comparisons and the many-body clock regime. Independent laboratories in Japan, the United States, Germany, France and China have built and compared such clocks, which for an experimentalist is the decisive test. On the chair's first question I would word the citation so that it rests on the lattice-trapping mechanism and its realisation, not on the record number alone, and not on clocks or combs in general. That separates it from 2005 (comb) and 2012 (control of single quantum systems) without saying that NIST, PTB, SYRTE and others contributed nothing. The name limit is also satisfied without any arbitrary cut: two names, identical in every ranking.
statement.case_against: The most serious objection, raised by Danielsson and Eriksson, is that the lattice clock may be better measurement rather than new physics, and that the fundamental-physics payoff (constants drifting, dark matter, geodesy) is largely prospective. I accept that the null results on constant variation are not a discovery. I do not accept that this disqualifies the clock, because the criterion is the original verified invention, not the downstream decisions of metrology bodies, and the many-body clock regime and the millimetre-scale redshift measurements are things nobody could do before. A second concern is that the two-name credit cannot reflect Lemonde, Takamoto, Derevianko, Ludlow and the NIST, PTB and SYRTE accuracy work, so the citation must claim only the concept and its first record-level realisations. A third is that the second has not been redefined. I note that and discount it.

responses.point: Danielsson holds B004 as the discovery with the clearest before and after, argues that the 2016 prize did not cover time-reversal-invariant Z2 insulators, and regards B041 as superb measurement science whose payoff is mostly promised and which he would not oppose.
responses.response: I take your 2016 argument seriously and I agree the Z2 classification is a new idea and not an application of Thouless and Haldane. My difficulty is the one you concede yourself: I must be absolutely sure we have identified the people who did the original work. Kane and Mele are clear. Molenkamp's experiment rested on the Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang HgTe proposal, and the 3D case is a separate claim by Hasan with Fu, Moore and Balents. Three names cannot cover this without an arbitrary cut. On the clock, I would answer that the discovery content is not only instrumental. A magic-wavelength lattice is a new way of holding many atoms in a regime where the clock transition is unperturbed, and it opened many-body clock physics and millimetre-scale redshift measurements. I understand that you would rank it second. Please tell the committee whether that is a reason to oppose it, or whether you could vote for it if the citation names the lattice concept.

responses.point: Eriksson prefers B017 with a three-name credit including Bistritzer, argues that the pairing mechanism is not part of the discovery, and says the lattice clock is very mature but a refinement in precision after 2005 and 2012.
responses.response: I accept the point that the cited discovery is the existence of the correlated phases and not their microscopic origin, and that the high-Tc comparison is fair. I also accept that Bistritzer belongs in the credit if this ballot is chosen. My remaining doubt is about time and about who is credited, not about the quality. Eight years is short for a result where the experimental credit is spread over Cao, Dean, Young, Yazdani, Efetov and others, and I cannot say we have found everyone who did the original experiment. On your question about novelty, the comb gave a way to count optical cycles and ion control gave single-particle clocks. Neither gave a way to remove the light shift for thousands of neutral atoms at once. The lattice clock reveals new behaviour in the form of collective coherence and shifts at 10^-18, which did not exist as an experimental regime before. Your own ranking of B041 as your first alternative suggests that we agree on its maturity. If the committee wants a condensed-matter prize in a few years, I would be glad to revisit B017.

responses.point: Mehlig prefers B027, lists B041 as his first alternative and would accept it as the likely consensus, but asks that the citation rest on the magic-wavelength mechanism and not on the record accuracy number.
responses.response: I agree completely with that request, and I have rewritten my citation so that the magic-wavelength trapping comes first and the 10^-18 level follows as the realisation. On B027, I appreciate the clean authorship of Halperin, Nelson and Young. My concern, which you also acknowledge, is that the 2016 citation to Kosterlitz and Thouless covered defect-driven transitions, and that experimental confirmation of the hexatic phase is mixed, with first-order melting in hard disks. Nature has given us clues in colloids, but not the single decisive experiment I look for. I would need to see that the experimental record settles the hexatic phase before I treated it as a prize-grade discovery. I do not see a reason that your analytic case fails in principle.

responses.point: Lindroth supports B041 and wants the citation to lead with the clocks themselves, while also naming the 10^-18 level, and she lists Lemonde, Takamoto and Derevianko as having claims on particular steps.
responses.response: I agree with the emphasis, and I am happy that the citation should lead with the optical lattice clock, with the magic-wavelength mechanism as the explanatory clause. I would disagree only mildly on the other names: Takamoto's 2005 demonstration was within Katori's group, so it belongs to the invention credited to Katori, and Lemonde and Derevianko contributed to the theory of shifts and the accuracy evaluation. That is precisely why the citation should not be broader than the concept and the first record-level realisations. I would also ask that the committee secretary confirm the no-recusal position you raised on B002, B034 and B042, because it bears on how freely we can discuss alternatives.

uncertainties: Whether the final citation can be worded so that it is distinct from the 2005 comb and 2012 single-quantum-system prizes and does not claim more than the concept and the first record-level realisations.
How much weight to give the accuracy work of Lemonde, Takamoto, Derevianko and the NIST, PTB and SYRTE groups when only two names are possible.
Whether Danielsson and Eriksson regard the discovery-versus-measurement distinction as a reason to oppose B041 or only as a reason to rank it second.
For B028, whether Blais can be excluded from a four-name list, and how close it sits to the 2025 prize; for B029, whether any two- or three-name credit is defensible from the record.
statement.conflict_note: I have no collaboration, institutional tie or personal relationship with Katori, Ye or any other credited person for B041. I share the Chalmers physics environment with Goran Johansson, whose work on superconducting circuits is adjacent to B028, and I therefore treat my views on B028 with caution; I also support his decision to discount his own B028 ranking. Mehlig and I are in neighbouring Gothenburg departments, with no specific collaboration. I have no recusal to declare.
